  "passage_text": "Not far from our camp at Hoiiing, on tlie plain torrarcls Lliari, I found a large stone
containing an inscription of Tsongkhapa’s time. It mentions, besides the names of the
reformer and one or txvo of his contemporaries, those of an ancient lama-ldng of Guge,
Byang-chub-’od, of the famous lama Kin-chen-bzang-j)o of the year 1000 A. D., and also
that of the Tabo monastery. This shoe's that in the 15th century people belieyed in
a connection between the Tabo monastery of Spiti, and the great priest-kings of
Guge.

From Horling, the high and beautiful snow mountains near the Tillage of Chang,
which belong to the group of the Purgyul peaks and are over 22,000 feet high, can be
seen. W e had already admired them on our way to Shipke, when we were much closer to
them (Plate X, a). At Namgya, I had heard the following ditty about them : —

Tise gangsTiyi rgyalpo yin
Vurgyul rii rgyalpo yin
Maspang mifisoyi rgyalpo yin.

“ Kailasa is the king of glaciers,

Purgyul is the king of mountains,

Manasarowar is the king of lakes.”

At Hoiiing the coolies from Chang, pointing towards the Purgyul group of mountains which is here called Gung-ri (perhaps the Ktingrang of the maps), said that on those
mountains was the fabulous ’aBa-yul, the abode of spirits. Its inhabitants are believed to
be numerous, but ordinary people can neither see nor hear them. It is only very good
men or lamas who are capable of perceiving anything. When such a pious man approaches that region of eternal snow, he hears the voices of its invisible denizens or the
barking of their ghostly dogs, but sees nothing. This tale reminds me strongly of a
passage which I had repeatedly found in inscriptions with reference to the Kailasa
mountains : — dgra hcom bzJiugs gnas Tise, ‘ Kailasa, the abode of those who have conquered all enemies’ {arhats). The ice mountains evidently are not only the abode of the
gods, but also that of the dead who, according to the belief of the Tibetans, have
acquired paradise.

We reached Lhari, the first village of Spiti, on the 28th July. Although this village
is possibly connected with the history of gNya-khri-btsam-po, the first king of Tibet, it is
nowadays a very poor place. It consists of only a few scattered houses. Above it, on
the side next the brook, there are the extensive ruins of an ancient castle, called Serlang,
the former abode of the Lhari people. Below the village there are very many ancient
rock-carvings, among which we note, in particular, the ibex and the svastika. One of the
carvings appears to represent the ‘ willow of the world ’ with its six branches and six
roots, one of the symbols of the pre-Buddhist religion of the people. Another symbol
appears to represent the sun and the moon. Dilapidated as Lhari is now-a-days, I cannot
escape the impression that it is a very ancient settlement.

On the 29th July, we marched to the famous Gelugpa monastery of Tabo which is
only three miles distant from Lhari (Plate XIV, a). When we were approaching it, I

said to Pindi Lai : “ You see, popular tradition connects this monastery witli Ein-clienbzang-po who lived 900 years ago, and an inscription at Holding showed us that such
traditions were also current in the 16th century. But what is the use of all these traditions ? We must have literary proof that a monastery actually goes hack to those early
days; if possible, we must have a document of those very times, on which it is plainly
stated that the erection of the monastery actually took place at that time. I wonder if
ever we shall be able to prove any such assumption!” As I said this, I little thought
that a few hours after, I should have ample proof in hand.

In the vicinity of the Tabo monastery are many rows of 108 small mchocl-rten, but
one of them numbered at least 216 (Plate XIV, b). They were the forerunners of the
mani walls in Western Tibet. Besides these rows, there are many ruined mchod-rten
round about, and countless rock carvings. The latter represent mostly the iljex and the
smstiha and are possibly of pre-Buddhist origin. On the hill side, almost like cave
dwellings, are the winter houses of the lamas.

The temple buildings are found on the plain above the river. They are surrounded
by a high mud wall. I made a plan of the whole establishment and these are some ot‘ the
measurements taken. Extreme length : 313 feet, 7 inches ; breadth 257 feet 3 inches.
Within this enclosure exist seven temple-halls, and a great number of mchod-rten. The
monks took me from one temple to another without showing me the principal hall. They
said that only a Commissioner (the highest personage they have ever heard of) could l)e
permitted to enter there. I tried in vain to convince them that, with regard to their
treasures, I was in as high an office as a Commissioner, until I produced two rupees.
Then the doors to their holy of holies were thrown open, and I presume that nothing of
interest was purposely concealed from us.

The principal hall is called rNam-par-snang-mdzad. The length of this hall with
additional apse is 63 feet, 14 inches and its breadth 34 feet, 10 inches. The principal
image is a white stucco statuette of rNam-par-snang-mdzad (Vairochana) consisting of four complete figures seated back to back (Plate XV, a). Along the walls, 6 or 7
feet above the ground, there are thirty-two raised medallions with exceedingly well executed stucco figures of life size (Plates XV, b ; XVI and XVII, b). Nobody in the monastery
at present knows whom they represent. But I am inclined to believe that they represent
the thirty-three Hindu gods.^ The figure of Ganela, which would make up the full
number, seems to have lost its original position above the door. It is now found on the
altar, below rNam-par-snang-mdzad (Plate XVII, a). One of the figures by the side
of the door was recently furnished with a new head like a modern Lamaist dancing
mask, the old head having been.lost (Plate XVII, b)."

  "passage_text": "The gTsug-lag-khang is a smaller hall with frescoes, to the left of the principal hall.
Most of the pictures refer to the story of Buddha’s life, beginning with the descent of the
white elephant from heaven. On both sides of the door were painted the four Lokapalas,
as we find them so often. On the right and left wall there was the medicine Buddha
with his followers, Sakya thub-pa, B.in-ehen-zla-ba ; Myang-ngan-med-mchog-dpal ; Ohosgrags-rgya-mthsoi-dpal ; gSer-bzang-dri-med ; mNgon-mkhyen-rgyal-po and mThsan-legs.
Most of the pictures in this hall were furnished with explanatory inscriptions in modern
Tibetan. Like all the remaining halls, it had apparently been renovated in a sweeping
way. All the ancient frescoes and inscriptions had been scratched off, and new pictures
painted on the old walls.

G

When we were at- Tabo, we met a native painter, who was prepared to renovate
everything. The monks of the monastery had been told that Government would undertake to pay for necessary repairs in their temples and had asked the Assistant Commis-
sioner to let them have the services of an artist. Accordingly, Mr. Howell, I.C.S., had
ordered a painter to go to Tabo and apply his art to its ancient walls, fortunately, he
had not yet started work in the principal hall, but in all the other halls, there remained
little which had not been destroyed either by him or by previous artists. I told the man
that he was on no account to touch the walls of the central hall, and when I met Mr.
Howell about a week later in Spiti, he promised to give strict orders that no further
attempt should be made to “improve ” this precious relic of the past.

The gSer-gyi-lha-khang is another picture hall to the left of the preceding one
AH the pictures in it are modern, and it has an inscription Oni mani padme hum in
.LaMhsa characters running round the four walls,

The dKyii-khang is a picture hall behind the preceding. As the roof is not ■watertight, the pictures have suffered much through leakage. The principal picture shows
rNam-par-snang-mdzad, but I could discover no inscriptions in it.

In Lha-khang-dkar-byung, a pictme hall behind the preceding, the central picture
shows Buddha with two disciples ; to the left of this group wo see Tsong-kha-pa. The
other pictures in this hall can no more be explained. There were no inscri])tions.

The picture hall Brom-ston was evidently named after tlic famous pupil of Atlsa,
called by that name, the founder of the bKa-gdams-pa sect. It is situated on the right
hand side of the Central Hall. It was probably erected in Brom-ston’s time, but nothing
remains of ancient relics, besides the interesting door of thamj -shiny (Deodar wood)
which is decorated with well executed carvings of Buddhist saints. The stylo of carving
is very different from the present Tibetan style, and is a distiuguishi.ng characteristic of
the half Indian Buddhism of the 11th century. This hall is without inscriptions and the
principal picture in it represents Buddha with his two disciples.

The seventh hall called Byams-pa-chen-moi-lha-khang contains a huge stucco statue
of Maitreya seated on a chair. The top of his head may be 18 to 20 feet above the
ground. This hall contains pictures of Tibetan architecture, perhaps four to five centuries
ago, such as the monastery of Tashilumpo (bKra-shis-lhun-po) and the Potala palace of

Natbang also\nis said to have been founded in the days, when the Tabo monastery was built.   "passage_text": "Then we hear of another embassy of Tibetans to Vikrama^ila, who were almost\nrobbed of their gold on the journey, and a religious assembly at this Indian monastery\nis described with its brilliant stars of wisdom and holiness who were all eclipsed by Ati^a.\nAs the Indian monks would not have allowed their master to leave the country, Atiia\ndisguised his intention of going to Tibet by saying that he was going on a pilgrimage to\nthe eight places of Buddhist sanctity,^ which pilgrimage took him to Nepal. He was\nmuch honoured by the king of that country, called Ananta-kirti, and performed various\nmiracles and acts of piety on the journey. Thus he made all the robbers who wished to\nassassinate him, dumb and motionless like statues, until he had passed by, and at times,\nhe lifted himself into the air a cubit above the saddle with a view to be distinguished\nfrom the others. A smile was ever on his face and Sanskrit mantras were ever on his lips.\nAt a deserted camping ground, he saw three puppies left uncared for. He took them in\nthe folds of his robes, saying •' Ah, poor little ones, I pity you,” and resumed his journey.\nThe breed of these puppies, says the historian, is still to be seen at Eva-sgrengs in Tibet.\n\nWhen the party entered Guge, they found one hundred horsemen all decoi-ated\nwith white ornamental equipments, sent by King Byang-chub-’od. The escort carried\nsmall flags and twenty white satin umbrellas. The band consisted of musical reeds, bagpipes, guitars, and other instruments. With sonorous and grave music, and uttering the\nsacred mantra, Om matii padme hum, they approached the holy sage to offer him a\nrespectful welcome in the name of the king of Guge. *\n\n^ THe eight great places o£ pilgrimage (Sanskrit mahasthana) aie 1st the Lninbini Garden (modem Eummindei in the Nepal\nTarai) where Buddha was born ; 2iii Bodh Gaya where he attained enlightenment ; 3rd the Deei’park (modern Samath) near\nBenares where he preached his first sermon ; 4th Kusinara (modern Kasia ?) where he reached Nirvana ; 5th th Jetarana\nnear Sravasti (modern Saheth-Maheth), where the great miracle took place, 6th Yaisaii (modem BasSrh) where he was fed by\na monkey ; 7th Samkasya (modem Sankisa) where he descended from heaven, and 8th Bajagriha (modern Eajgii‘) where he\nsubdued the wild elephant. [ Ed. ]\n\n^ This reception seems to be represented among frescoes in monasteries of those times.\n\nH 2\n\nAti^a had never yet tasted tea, and the first cup on Tibetan soil was offered him\nwith the following solemn words ; “ Venerable sage, permit me to make an offering of\nthis celestial drink which contains the essence of the wishing tree I” Ati^a said :\n“ This curious cup of precious material contains an elixir of the wishing tree.\nWhat is the name of this drink which you prize so much ? ” The Tibetans answered :\n“ Venerable sir, it is called tea. We do not know that the tea plant is eaten, but\nthe leaves are churned in warm water, and the soup is drunk. It has many properties ! ” Thereupon Ati^a, who could pay compliments like any French abb6, remarked :\n“ So excellent a beverage as tea must have originated from the moral merits of the monks\nuf Tibet!”\n\nThe Manasarowar Lake pleased Ati4a so much that he stayed there for seven days.\nThen he proceeded to mTho-lding, the capital of Guge, where he was received by the\nking with due honours. Although all the lamas and noblemen rose respectfully when\nAti^a approached them, the old lama, Ein-chen-bzang-po, would not rise, partly from\n■envy, partly from weakness. But then Ati4a displayed his intellectual armour in\nsuch a brilliant way before the old monk that even he was conquered and ready to sit\nat the feet of the newcomer.^ After a residence in Guge of two years, Ati^a proceeded\n^to Central Tibet. He died at Nyethang near Lhasa at the age of seventy-three in the\nyear 1053 A.D. The founding of the so-called half-reformed sects of Lamaism was\ndue to his exertions. The most important of them is the bKa-gdams-pa sect. It was\nin monasteries of this sect that Tsong-kha-pa studied, before he started the great reform\nmovement which ended in the creation of the Ge-lug-pa sect. The object of all these\nreformations was not, as is often supposed, to go back to the early Buddhism as it was\npreached by Gautama, but to build up a church which represented the doctrines of the\nMahayana school of Buddhism in a pure form. The doctrines of N agarjuna were propounded by all the great teachers of Tibet. But the Kala-chakra philosophy with its\nmonotheistic tendencies was also favoured by them.\n\nOn the 10th August, we travelled to the southern end of the lake, and then along\nIts western shore, and at sunset we arrived at bKor-rdzod (map Karzok. Plate XXIII).\nThe sudden appearance of the monastery in that barren desert was such a surprise that\nit was at first difficult to believe in its reality. On this march, the Tibetan fauna was\nmuch in evidence. There wore large herds of rhyang (wild asses which look like mules),\nand one of the rhyang came quite close to us and watched our caravan passing by.\nThere were very many hares and marmots which did not show any signs of fear, and\nalso the beautiful tail-less rats of Tibet looked at us curiously from behind many a stone.\nWhilst animal life was thus well represented on dry land, I could not discover any\nliving being in the water of the lake. But as aquatic plants were plentiful it attracted\n-wild geese and ducks, of which we saw a good number. As Drew says, gulls have their\nbreeding ground on an island in the lake.   "passage_text": "blue-green water, and dunes of yellow sand combine to make a picture like those sublime\n-quiet landscapes, which have become familiar through Sven Hedin’s Tibetan sketches.\n\nThe first European who visited the lake was Trebeck in 1820. Cunningham gives\nthe legend of the lake which explains its unusual name. W e heard the same legend at\nbKor-rdzod. Although the tale is quite without a point, Cunningham says that it is as\ngood as many a Greek tale. The word Thsomo means ‘lake,’ and iJw’i is an ex-\n■clamation used by people when driving yaks. According to the tale, an old woman\n■ came riding on a yak and made the animal wade into the water. She was shouting Min\nall the time, and was finally drowned together with her yak. It is strange that Trebeck\ndoes not make any mention of a monastery on the lake, although he travelled along its\nwestern shore. All the same, the convent must have been in existence in his time, for in\nan inscription which I found on one of the many mani walls which line the lake shore,\nthe expression dGon-snying, ancient monastery, was used with reference to it. These\nma'^i walls extend to about two miles in both directions from the monastery (Plate\nXXIV, a) . The votive tablets on these walls contained the names of several chiefs of the\nPubshu nomads who have their residence close to the monastery. Of royal Ladakhi\nnames, I found only two mentioned, those of the two last independent rulers of Ladakh.\nBut another tablet near the monastery contained a very beautiful hymn on Tibet, especially\nits western parts. This hymn was more of a geographical than historical character.\nW e took an impression of this inscription, and I had to make an eye-copy in addition.\n\nI visited the monastery next morning and was disappointed to hear that it was a\nmodern structure, between fifty and sixty years old.^ The old monastery stood on the\nbrook, below the present site ; but not a trace of it now remains. The few ancient\nimages and other articles of worship were taken up to the present building. Among\nthe antiquities pointed out to us, were several miniature mchod-rien of the usual type.\n• Of all the stucco figures, and of a fine wood-carving in sandal wood, which represented\nPadma-sambhava with two of his fairy friends, it was asserted that fifty or sixty years ago\nthey had been brought up here from gSham, Lower Ladakh. I suspect that these Eubshu\npeople bought up the entire contents of a ruined monastery in Lower Ladakh. The principal stucco figure represents Buddha with two disciples, and another Padma-sambhava.\nThe names of the other images, I did not try to ascertain, because the history of their\ndate and origin will always remain obscure. I may mention here, that outside, near the\nsite of the ancient monastery, I found a relievo representing Padma-sambhava, carved\non a beautiful slab of snow-white quartz. I was greatly tempted to carry it off, but it\nwould have been too heavy. One of the clay pots in the bKor-rdzod monastery reminded\n,me of the stone age of Europe. It had evidently been made by plastering the inside of\na basket with clay and then burning the basket. All the books at this monastery were\nmodern Tibetan prints.\n\nThe neck ornament of a man at bKor-rdzod who acted as Lambardar, attracted my\nA attention, because it was of cruciform shape, and could at first sight be taken for a\nChristian ornament. He said, he had excavated it from a high hiU in the neighbourhood.\n\n^ A picture of the old monastery is found in Schlagintweits* B&isen in Indien und Soohasien Jena 1872-18.\n\nI bought it from him for two rupees. It was made of a mixture of metals, similar tO'\nthe Indian kliansl. It was a plain cross with beams of equal length, and at the end of\neach beam was found a double spiral as an ornament. As I was told by another man\nfrom Eubshu, there are ruins of ancient settlements and watercourses all over the\ncountry. They are found on high bill s in Eubshu, and are ascribed to a tribe of Mon,\nthe pre-Tibetan inhabitants of the country. These Mon must have been marvels of\nendurance. How they could have cultivated fields at those altitudes, is a mystery. The\nbarley fields of the bKor-rdzod monastery are in Mr. Drew’s opinion the highest in the\nworld (Plate XXII, b). But those of the Mon settlers must have been higher still.\nAccording to Survey maps,^ the altitude of bKor-rdzod is 16,600 feet, but according to\nDrew it is only 15,000 feet high. Drew gives the following numbers with regard to this\nlake : length 16 miles, breadth 3 to 5 miles ; depth 248 feet. It may sound incredible\nthat there should have been fields still higher than the present fields of bKor-rdzod whose\nharvest sometimes fails. But I remember that also on one of my former journeys, in\nZangskar, I came across the ruins of a Dard settlement at an altitude where it was icy\ncold even in summer."
}

  "passage_text": "Whilst we were encamped at bKor-rdzod, the chief of the Eubshu nomads visited\nme, and to entertain him, I showed him the pictures of my “History of Western Tibet.”\nHe enjoyed them thoroughly, but he was struck with emotion on seeing the portrait\nof the ex-king of Ladakh with his son and retinue. As tho cx-king was married to his\nown sister, this picture represented some of his nearest relation, and he implored mo\nnot to go away without making him a present of it. There remained no alternative\nfor me but to tear the picture out of the book, and hand it over to him. It was\nhowever, fortunate for us, to have placed under obligation sucli an important personage through this little present. Por, if we had not been in his favour, it would\nprobably have taken a long time before the nomads found yaks for us. As matters\nstood, the yaks turned up in good condition next morning. In the same way, it was\nalso our good fortune to have met with the Assistant Commissioner in Spiti. Otherwise\nwe should certainly have had diflGLculty in getting transport animals from Spiti to the\nlake. It must be remembered that animals as well as men are scarce in tlicse frontier\nregions, that the roads are dMcult, if not dangerous, and that these frontier people\ncan hardly be reached by any authority. Last year, as Mr. Ho^vell told me, transport\nwas absolutely refused to a traveller in Spiti, who obtained it only by using desperate\nmeans.\n\nAs we have been travelling on yaks for some time, and as we have before us many\nmore miles of yak riding, it seems the proper place to say a few words about these interesting Tibetan animals. The first yak ride we had on our way hack from Shipke,\nand the second on the journey from Spiti to the lake. All those yaks had rings through\ntheir noses, and could in a way be controlled by them, for it requires great anger on tho\npart of the yak to make him indifferent to the pain which would be caused by his tearing himself free and running away. But the yaks which we received for our journey\n\n^ Surrey Map of 1874. Sheet 46 gives Karzofc as 14,960 ft. [Ed.]\n\nPlate XXV.\n\na. Nomads’ camp on Lake Thsomo Riri.\n\nb. Yaks on the shore of Lake Thsomo Riri.\n\nfrom bKor-rclzod to Nyoma on the Indus, and from Nyoma to rGya in Ladakh, 'vrere\nwithout this last touch of culture, a nose-ring. They had neither saddles, nor bridles,\nnor even nose-rings, they were absolutely undefiled products of nature. When I asked the\nnomads why even this last remnant of civilisation was not found on them, they said that\nthis particular breed of yaks did not possess any noses. I was pitying the poor creatures\nfor whom the roses had no scent, when I noticed that two little holes could he distinguished above the mouth. That in these circumstances it was no easy matter to use the\nyaks for riding, can well he imagined. In fact, their management was so difficult, that\nI would have gladly renounced this doubtful pleasure altogether, if the ratified air of\nthose altitudes had not compelled me to use these uninviting beasts. When I was tired, I\nwould tell one of the nomads to get me a yak for riding. Then all the men would run in\nfront of the herd of yaks they were driving, shouting at them and waving their arms in the\nair, to make them understand that they were wanted to stop. A single one could never\nbe made either to stop or to start. Their esprit de corps was so strong that they insisted\non doing everything together. Now, when the herd was stopped, one of the unladen yaks\nwas singled out for my use and seized by the horns. Naturally he disliked this treatment,\nand whilst he was dancing round the man, I was supposed to fly through the air and\n'drop on the yak’s back. As soon as I had reached my seat and seized its mane, the\nnomad would let go the horns, and off went the yak galloping up and down the hillside,\nuntil he had found his natural equilibrium, when he joined the herd again. The nomads\nhad the kindness to select for me the least savage of their yaks, but the Khalasi and\nKhansaman had to take what remained, and that led often to exciting performances.\nI still see the Khalasi seated on the tail and hindquarters (for he had failed to drop\ndown in the middle part of the animal) of a furious yak, which charged up and down\nwith him on very uneven ground on the Thaglang Pass. Then, when the yak had found\nhis place in the caravan of snorting beasts, he would look out for another yak, his adversary, and poke him with his horns. The opponent, naturally offended by this act of\nspecial attention, would pay it back in the same coin. In these continual fights, the\nyaks knocked a lock off one of our boxes, made holes in several others, and smashed the\ntripod of our camera. That they did not smash our own legs, was due to the continual\ncare with which we watched these fights. Whenever one’s own yak was charged by his\nadversary, one had to lift high the threatened leg, and join in the struggle by using one’s\nstick and umbrella. There was, however, one weapon which was respected by all the\nyaks. That wns the stone whip of Eubshu. We were now in the centre of a large treeless country, and thus it is not to be wondered at, that even the whip should be a stone\nimplement. It was an oblong stone, three to four pounds in weight, with which the\nyaks were hammered on their hind quarters, whenever they showed signs of laziness.\nCuriously, the a.TiiTna.1s seemed to fear the sight of this stone implement more than its\nweight. The one I was riding on was often energetically hammered by a nomad behind\nme, a treatment which he endured with the utmost indifference. But the moment he saw\nanother nomad using his stone against a yak in front of him, he shuddered with terror.\nWhen the hammering failed to make an impression, the stones were thrown at the yaks.\n\nOnce, tlie Khalasi had such a stone flung at his leg, which caused him to complain\nbitterly, as he was an official personage, hut the nomads explained that it was intended\nfor the yak."

Its depth is 67 feet\naccording to Drew. Its water is brackish, like that of the Thsomo Diri. There is no\npermanent habitation on its shore, but many stone walls have been erected by the\nnomads who often have their encampment on this lake. The scenery round about is\nvery grand and of the same character as on the Thsomo E.iri.\n\nOn the 13th August, we had our camp near Raldrong, where the Phuga brook enters\nthe Indus. Opposite the confluence are the ruins of a Mon village. This is probably\nthe deserted village mentioned by the late Dr. Shawe in his letter of the 19th J uly 1900,\nin which he advised me to visit Nyoma and surroundings. Dr. Shawe wrote as follows:\n“ Some miles west of Nyoma are said to be the remains of an old Mon village, where I was\ntold boxes, household utensils, and coins have been found (apparently in graves). Unfortunately I did not hear of this till I had left and was across the Indus, or I would\nhave made enquiries. Coins should prove interesting and instructive,” From the left\nbank of the Indus we could see deserted fields in terraces, a group of houses, and walls.\nAs, however, the distance from Nyoma was fully ten miles, and we were perfectly ex--\nhausted from our long desert journey, I could not manage to visit the site. In Nyoma\nI tried to obtain some of the articles found by the people at this deserted village, but\nthey pretended not to possess any such things.\n\nOn the 14!th August, we marched to Nyoma, where we had our camj) on the loft bank\nof the Indus. Pindi Lai and myself crossed the Indus on a little raft of inflated skins.\nThe river journey on this raft, where four men had to sit motionless on a single square\nyard, occupied fuUy half an hour. Pindi Lai got a slight touch of the sun, and a\nsevere headache prevented him from enjoying the shade of the first willows after Kaze\nin Spiti, to which he had been looking forward. He was, however, bravo enough to take\nsome photos of objects of interest.\n\nThe elevation of Nyoma (Nimu, Nima, etc., on maps) is given as about 14,000 feet\nby Drew. This is certainly exaggerated. It could hardly be more than 13,000. Dro\"W\nmentions the few large wfllow trees of great age at the village. They would not be\nfound, we may be sure, at an elevation of 14,000. Besides, we saw very many young\nand thriving ones. Before speaking of our own experiences, let me quote Dr. Shawe’s\nobservations according to his letter of the 19th July 1906. He says : “ Here (at\nNyoma) are very fine remains of a castle and old town on the top of a rock (Plate XXVI, a)..\nThe buildings all more or less destroyed except the temple which is said to be of the\nsame date as the rest, and contains a fine lot of small brass idols and other temple\nutensils. The town is said to have been built by bDe-skyong-mam-rgyal (c. 1730 A.D.)\nwhose name I also found on a man,i wall. The only other king’s name was Don-grub -\nrnam-rgyal (1790 1841), but there are many old maijA walls, both of the ordinary and of\nthe shelf type. On the plain behind the rock are extensive remains of a village whiclt\n\ntlie. jjeople said, was of the same date as the castle, but which appeared to me much older\nfrom the style of building, also two or three \" step mchod-rten'\" but no ladder in the\nmiddle of sides (like those of. the AlcM-mhhar-gog carvings). One old mchod-rten of the\nordinary type, now fast falling to pieces, had a small door at either end, some three feet\nhigh, and the interior was very finely decorated with paintings of Buddha’s temptation,\nhis subduing demons, etc. The decorations of the ceiling were in relievo. It is by far\nthe finest piece of vnchod~rten decoration I have seen yet. The only rock carving I\ncould find was a migmang (kind of chessboard) on a boulder, but no inscriptions on\nrocks at all.”\n\nAs we see, Dr. Shawe himself did not feel satisfied with the people’s statement that\nthe town of Nyoma was built by bDe-skyong-rnam-rgyal. He found distinct signs of\nan earlier origin. The old types of mchod-rten especially, and the fact that one of them\nwas beautifully decorated inside, point to an age of at least 900 to 1,000 years. I went\nto examine the temple which occupies the highest position in the now deserted town\non the rook and belongs to the ’aBrug-pa order of monks. Since Dr. Shawe had been\ntold that the temple was built in the 18th centruy, the monks had altered their opinion,\nand I was told that it dated from the days of King Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal (c. 1600). I was,\nhowever, not satisfied with an assertion which possibly had no real foundation and\nasked the monks to show me proof of this assertion. Then they brought me a book\nwhich had been dedicated to the monastery by Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal and actually contained\na dedication sheet on which the names of the king and his illustrious queen bSkal-bzang\ncould be distinctly read. It is difficult to believe that there was nothing before Seng-ge-rnam-rgyaTs\ndays in a pleasant vaUey like Nyoma, and ancient mchod-rten distinctly point to a time,\nearlier than this king.   "passage_text": "On this picture we see a number of whitewashed houses, one or two stories high.\nThey look exactly like the present Ladakhi houses and also have a red or black band\nround the roof, just as the present monasteries have. Then we see the inside of the\nroyal kitchen with five or six people busy at work, and the male and female members of\nthe royal family in separate rooms. Below the houses are painted two processions which\napproach the buildings from right and left. The men on the right hand side are riding\non mules or rkyangs, and those on the left are walking, carrying presents, perhaps tribute.\nThe. chief value of the picture lies in the fact that the costumes of those times ar(i painted\nso well. Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal is the king who is credited by popular tradition with the\nintroduction of the Ladakhi type, of dress, as it remained unchanged down to the time\n\nI\n\nof the Pogra war. In a collection of Tibetan proverbs which I acquired from a man from\nrGya some years ago, and which is among the manuscripts brought to Simla, there is\na proverb which refers to the change of dress under this king. There it is stated that\nthe king, whose name S6nQ~y€ means “ lion,** said that he was willing to honoui his\nsubjects by giving them one of his ears ; thus the men received the high black cap,\ncalled s6ng-g6 Ttioi-wbchog, “ lion’s ear ” which I finci pictured by Drew. The same proverb informs us that the great tiger lama {sTag means a tiger) favoured the women by\ngiving them his spotted skin. Thus the dark blue dress of the Ladakhi women with its\nred and yellow spots was introduced. The picture in the Nyoma monastery does not,\nhowever, show the new fashion, having possibly been painted before its introduction.\nAll the male persons wear turbans, as was the fashion in Western Tibet from c. 1000\nA.D. downwards. The royal ladies are distinguished by their rich herags, fillets\nof leather which are covered with precious stones. Although I have not yet been able\nto trace them on pictures earlier than c. 1530 A.D., I am convinced that this fashion\ngoes back to examples of old Indian art, where the Nagas and Nagis were represented\nby a human figure with a snake growing out of the back and over-topping their heads.\nThe herag of the Ladakhi women which begins in the middle of the back and becomes\nbroader over the head, looks like the representation of a snake. Perhaps the Ladaklii\nwomen wished to look like Nagis, because these water fairies were famous for their\nbeauty.\n\nWe spent Sunday, the 15th August, on the left bank of the Indus river, opposite\nNyoma, and resumed our journey on Monday the 16th. Our next aim was Leh, and as\nthe road along the Indus river was impracticable at that time of the year, I had to decide\nwhich of the two other roads we were to take, the road by Drangtse (map Tankse), or\nthat by Phuga. As regards the Drangtse road, it attracted me much on account of a description Dr. Shawe had given me of it. The Phuga road, on the other hand, would take\nus to rGya, the antiquities of which I had previously examined. I decided for the latter\nroute, but I will quote Dr. Shawe’s letter on the Drangtse road to show the reader what\nwe missed. He says in his letter of the 19th July 1906 ; —\n\n“ I was told yesterday by one of the men that at Sakti you only visited the newest of\nthe three old- castles — the oldest being a mile or two up the valley. I am sorry I did\nnot know when there. I saw few, if any, rock carvings in Sakti, except a migmmig (see\np. 67) on a boulder. At Drangtse is an old castle and village on top of a rock, destroyed\nby the Dogras. It is in very fair preservation, some of the streets being quite recognisable.\nAround Drangtse are numbers —thousands— of rock carvings of the usual ibex and yak\ntype, but no Indian buHs, as far as I saw. At first I thought there were no inscriptions,\nand nobody could or would tell of any ; but later, on top of a large rock or boulder, I found\na number of carvings of some of which I enclose original copies. One, a ehorten, had a\nlong inscription beneath in letters which appear to be mostly, but not entirely, Tibetan,\nand on another boulder a line in Persian characters. Two or three carvings of crosses\n\n^ J UtMuhco and p. 240 .\n\nwere rather interesting ; I give copies. Another carving about a mile out, on the road to\nPangkong (lake) of a stag hunt, thus [drawing]. A large and rough outline of\nBuddha on a rock seems to be fairly new— newer than some chortens on the same rock.\nI found no kings’ names or votive inscriptions on manis at Drangtse, and the clay tablets\nwere all of the chorten type, without letters, as far as I could see. Ohushol yielded nothing\nof antiquarian interest, and I found nothing more till I got to Nyoma on the Indus. ”"

I may\nremark that he was the first traveller w^ho ever passed through this district with\nhis eyes open to objects of archaeological value. In 1906, 1 had travelled with Dr. Shawe\nas far as Chemre {IGe-hde) where we had investigated the monastery built by Seng-gernam-rgyal. We became thoroughly convinced that there had existed a monastery\npreviously on the same site. I went up the valley from Chemre to Sakti on a hurried visit,\nand as Dr. Shawe points out, in his letter, visited only the latest of three ancient castles.\nThe first European traveller who visited the Chemre-Sakti valley, was Moororoft in 1820.\nHe also noticed the “ fort ” of Sakti which was already in ruins in his time. What he\nsaw was also “ the newest of the three old castles. ” Thus, the two older ones still remain\nto be investigated. Moorcroft^ says : “ On the face of the mountain, forming part of the\neastern limit of the valley, stood the fort of Sakti, a pile of buildings surrounded by a\nwall and towers, the whole built of granite blocks cemented with clay ; the houses were\nunroofed, but the walls were mostly standing. This fortress was evidently intended to\ncommand the northern entrance of the valley, but it was taken and dismantled by the\nKalmaks nearly two centuries ago and has never been repaired. ”\n\nThe Kalmaks who dismantled this fortress, were evidently the Mongols and Lhasa\nTibetans under Thse-dbang of Galdan, who after having beaten the Ladakhis in the\nbattle of Zhamarting, besieged them in the fortress of Basgo. On their way to Basgo,\n1646, they probably destroyed all the fortresses of eastern Ladakh, As we learn from\nMoorcroft, the Chemre-Sakti valley was under the command of the famous Ladakhi minister Bang-kha who ruled over seventy villages. The family of these Bang-khas evidently\nhad the hereditary office of ‘defender of the eastern gates of Ladakh. Their principal\ncastle was the gSer-khri-mkhar of Igu, in the neighbouring valley, where there are many\nancient ruins, among them walls with frescoes in front of huge carvings of Bodhisattvas.\nOne of the great generals of bDe-ldanr nam-rgyal (c.l630 A.D.) was a Bang-kha-pa\nfrom Igu. At present, there is not much\nremaining in the temple hall ; one of the frescoes is, however, of unusual interest\nas it represents Gog-bzang-lha-mo, the mother of Kesar and one of the great pre-\nBuddhist deities of the Ladakhis. This picture is probably of ancient origin, although\nit had apparently been renovated from time to time. It was painted at a time wheu\nBon -po art was largely influenced by Buddhist art. The complexion of the goddess is a-,\nbeautiful white, whilst her hair is black. The hair is raised over the forehead and\nfurnished with a ribbon and a diadem of pearls. Her ear ornaments (probably shells)\nare white and spiral-shaped, and her dress is white with blue and red seams. In her\nhand she carries a white cup.\n\nOpposite the monastery, there is a hill with cave dwellings, probably the mostancient inhabited locality at Meru. It is called ^aho (‘ Oaves ).\n\nK\n\nThe place where the ixihabitaats of Mem had to liye before they built their present\nhouses in the bottom of the yalley, is a hill spur on the right bank of the rGya riyer\nwhere there are extensire ruins of houses. As has been stated aboye, during the\nascendency of the Ladakhi kings people were not allowed to liye among the fields,\nprobably to prevent their trespassing too much on yaluable ground. But, as we learnt\nfrom Moorcroft’s account of rGya, the lofty sites on the top of rocks were already\npartly abandoned daring the times of the last king, Thse-dpal -don-grub -rdo-rje-rnamrgyal (1820 A..])). Prom his account it appears that at Meru also people hyed in their\npresent houses in 1820.\n\nSeveral miles below Mlera, the xGrya brook discharges into the Indus, and at this\nplace is situated the village of TJbshi (Hoorcroft’s UhsKi). In this village we noticed\nseveral meJiod-rten of great age which were known to the inhabitants as mcliocl-rten\nof the Mons. We examiued the interior of one of them and found the walls inside\ncovered with ancient frescoes which were apparently painted with two colours only,\nindigo blue and brownish red. There were any number of rows of figures of blue\ncomplexion seated cross-legged, Their garments were white with red scams. The\nlarger pictures in the centre of the four walla were too far gone to allow of any identification. The headdress of these blue figures was somewhat unusual ; it looked as if\nthe ends of a long hair-pin projected on each side. Later on, when I had examined\nseveral more similar frescoes at other ancient sites, I came to the conclusion that\nthe TJhshi pictures represent Hagas {Klu), and that these ancient mchod-rten may\nhe Bon-po, and not Buddhist, structures.\n\nWe spent the night of the 20th and the 21st August at Martsclang. Hero I\nhad a pleasant surprise ia meeting one of the Leh mission ladies, Mivss Scliurtcr,\nvho had travelled through the desert wilds of Bubsbu from Kyelang to Leh, accom 2 )anied\nonly by two Ohristiau Tibetans from the former place. I might bare caught her\nup much earlier, if she had not been alarmed by rumours of the ajopmoach of a very\nuntrustworthy sportsman (myself !) which caused her to make double marches to\nescape him.\n\nMartselang is situated at the lower end of the Shang valley (the Qhanga of\nHoorcroft), which eontaiiis the Hemis monastery. This monastery which was\nbuilt by king Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal only about 300 years ago, has acquired quite\n-unusual fame among European visitors to Ladakh on account of its devil-dances.\nThese are performed here in June (originally probably on the occasion of the summer\nsolstice), a convenient time for Europeans to attend them, whilst most of the other\nmonasteries have the same performance in winter. The monastery was also frequently\nreferred to fifteen or eighteen years ago, when the Bussian traveller Notovitch surprised\n\"the world by stating that he had found in it a copy of a new Christian gospel written\nin Pali. A great deal of learned correspondence then took place which proved that\nHotovitch’s extraordinary find was a forgery. Although the Hemis monastery is not very ancient, yet it contains images\nof a type which is found only in monasteries of the 10th or 11th century. When the\nmonks are asked to state the place of origin of such statues, they say that they were\nbrought here from Lhasa. I wonder if that can be true. It seems to me that a more\nlikely explanation is that these images were brought here from Meru, which is, as\nalready stated, the “ mother ” monastery of Hemis."

along the road, from this place to Ohushod, these mchod-rten were much in evidence.

Khrigtse, E/anbirpur, and Sheb, where they are numerous. At Eanbirpm’, I remember
having seen even several specimens of the ladder type in fair preservation. The conviction that we are travelling here on ancient Buddhist ground, grew very strong on
me. It is not impossible that the present village and monastery of Khrigtse are identical with the castle of Khri-btsegs-’abum-gdugs mentioned before Srong-btsan-sgam-po,
who was the first Buddliist king of Tibet, and with the monastery of Khri-rtse
mentioned under King Mes-ag thsoms (706 — 755 A.D). Local names in Sanskrit which
are found here and there in Ladakh, date from the times of this more Indian than
Tibetan form of Buddhism. The names of Meru, and Sakti (Skr. SaMi) have already
been mentioned. I may add the names of Muni and Kanika (= Kanishka ? ) in
Zahgskar, and Tar (Skr. Tdrd, on account of the Svayambhu Taras at that place), Hari
rtse (Summit of Hari). The greater part of the Ladakhi local names are certainly
Tibetan, but not a few are of Dard origin. In connection with the latter statement let
me point to the many names which have the Bard word hem (Skr. hima) or hen
“ snow,” as one of their component parts, mz., Hembabs (Bras), Henasku, Hema la,
Hemis. Of other pla inl y Bard names like Hanu, Hunupatta, Garkunu, Chanegund,
Hibti, Esu, et(j., I cannot yet explain the etymology. The name Banblrpur is a modern
Bogra name.® A few ancient Indian personal names also have been preserved in
folklore and inscriptions. Thus, the ruined castle opposite Stag-sna is called the castle
of king Surgamati (Skr. Sury-amati, “Sun-mind”) and among the old royal names on
inscriptions at Khalatse we find Shirima (Skr. Srlmdn) and (probably) Satyamati
(“Truth-mind”), besides several others.

When riding along the left bank of the Indus river, we could see the villages,
castles and monasteries on the right bank, a visit to many of which would amply
reward archseological research. T'he conical hill of the Khrigtse monastery always

He spent two years at Leh, and as he was a very keen and intelligent observer,\nhis description of the kingdom is of unique interest. But when they were ready to tender their allegiance,\ntheir offer was declined by the East India Company. How different the fate of Ladakh\nwould have been, had it been accepted. Moorcroft had no doubts then, that Ladakh\nwould soon be swallowed up by Russia, for the Prime Minister showed him a letter from\n■the Emperor of Russia to the king of Ladakh whiclx had been brought there by a Jew,\nsix years before. Moorcroft and Trebeck became eye-witnesses of some little warfare\nbetween the Ladakhis and Baltis, and between the Ladakhis and the Kulu State ; they\nalso saw the seditious placard at Leh, in which the unsatisfactory rule of the king\nwas contrasted with the excellent rule of his predecessor, his brother, who had died\n.young. The streets are disposed without any order,\nand form a most intricate labyrinth, and the houses are built contiguously, and run into\neach other so strangely, that from without it is difficult to determine the extent of each\nmansion. It is true that even then some\nhouses existed outside the walls, but the town proper was enclosed by a fortified wall .\nThe two large bazaars which form such a conspicuous feature of the present to’W'n of\nLeh were not yet in existence. As popular tradition asserts, the large bazaar of Leh\nwas laid out by the Dogras after the war of 1834-18-12, and the new bazaar was made in\n1897 by Captain Trench, British Joint Commissioner. I have been told, the Schlagintweits give a very minute descrijotion of Leh as it was in 1856, when the large bazaar\nwas aheady in existence. Where this description is to be found, I have not been able\nto trace. A few remains of the walls of Leh are found right in the middle of the present\ntown, where there is also one of the ancient crooked gates. This gate, which is a little\nnorth-east of the great mosque at the end of the bazaar, marks the extent of the former\ntown towards the south. All those houses which are found between the rNam-rgyal\nrtse-mo Hill and this gate, belong to the old town of Leh, of Moorcroft’s time. He makes\nspecial mention only of three conspicuous buildings, viz., the royal palace, the Chamba\n(.Byams-pa, i.e., Maitreya) and the Chenresi (sPyan-ras-gzigs, i.e., Avalokite^vara)\nMonasteries. These three buildings are still in existence, and will be referred to in due\ncourse. The folio-wing conspicuous buildings of the old town must also have been in\nexistence in Moorcroft’s time, although he does not make any reference to them.\nThe house Blon-po (“ Minister ’ ’) is situated directly below the castle, on the south-west\ncorner ;the dGon-pa-so-ma, (New Monastery) is situated on the south-eastern corner of the\nsame castle. It is the scene of the devil-dances which were witnessed by Moorcroft.\nBoth these buildings can be distinguished on Trebeck’s picture of Leh. Below the\nd6on-pa-so-ma and the Byams-pa monasteries, is situated the mEhar-chung {“ the little\nPalace”), and exactly below the latter the ruined site of the house (“ Prime\n\nMinister ”), possibly the very same house in which Moorcroft was received in audience by\nthe then Prime Minister. Skulls from Dard graves, Leh.\n\nTo-go-ohe used to be au official who ranked between a minister and a Orong-dpon, or\nmayor. The present representative of the To-go-che is Munshi dPal-rgyas, the chronicler\nof Ladakh. To the west of his house we find the house Orong-dpon or “ Mayor,” and\nbelow it the old Byams-pa (Maitreya) monastery. From the\nchronicles of Ladakh we learn that a “ new palace” was built above the sPyan-ras-gzigs\nMonastery during the reign of King Thse-dpal-rnam-rgyal. That would account for\none of those buildings. During the reign of the same king mention is also made of a\nTheg-cJien-gong-ma Hall.” As, however, nothing definite is s.nid with regard to its\nsituation, we do not know whether it is a room in the old castle or the building shown\non Trebeck’s sketch between the large royal palace and the “ New Palace,” behind the\nAvalokite^vara Monastery.\n\nWe could not possibly examine all the antiquities of Leh within four weeks, but\nwe did some work, and I now wish to describe what we found.\n\nWe were just entering Leh, when I heard that somebody had again opened the\nancient Dard graves near the Teu-gser-po, about two miles above the Commissioner’s compound in the Leh valley. This is the same site on which Dr. Shawe and myself had done\nsome excavation work in 1903. As I did not wish anybody else to take away the more\nimportant objects of interest, I asked Mr. Schmitt of the Moravian Mission to go with\nme to the graves on the 23rd August. This we did, and the two Christian boys who\naccompanied us jmoved very useful in opening the graves, which involved very hard\nw'ork. The roof of the grave is more than a yard below the present level of the ground.\nIt consists of largo unhewn stones of rectangular shape, each about 1-| yards long, and a\nfoot or so broad. The w^aUs of the grave consist of masonry of unhewn stones. It is\nabout two yards long, yards broad, and at least six feet deep. W e had not yet\nreached the bottom, when we stopped our excavations. Originally the roof of the\ngrave was probably above the ground. Later on, the deposits accumulated and buried\nit. But destruction did not set in, as I believe, until a field was made above it. Then,\nthe continual flood of the irrigation water destroyed all the woodwork and many of the\nbronze implements began to oxydize. I suppose that the Leh graves originally contained wooden boards just like those at rG-ya.\n\nThe grave contained clay pots of various sizes, a few entire, but most of them in\nfragments (Plate XXVIII, a). The largest pot, of which only fragments came to light,\nmay have had a height of three feet, and its diameter was probably not much- less. The\nsmaller pots, which were rarer than the large ones, had a height of 10 to 15 cm. There\nwere also small, saucer-like vessels of clay, probably lamps. The natives who were with\nus at once asserted, that the pottery of the grave was distinctly different from present\ndav Tibetan pottery.   "passage_text": "Dr. Sliawe in his house, and photographed by Miss Duncan.^ This time we coiilcl not\nfind a single pot with painted designs in the grave. But there were linear ornaments\nimpressed on several of them. The only places in Ladakh, besides the graves, where\nsim i lar hand-made pottery with dark red ornaments has been found, are the ancient\nruined castles of sBalu mkhar and Alchi mkhar gog. A plate showing such pottery\nis reproduced in my article “ Arohseological Notes on sBalu mJchcir” * Another\ncollection of such ornamental sherds was made at Alchi mkhar gog on our expedition\nand brought to Simla. These ornaments are all of a very primitive type. They consist of spirals, ladders, and a zigzag band ; and occasionally there arc bunches of lines\nwhich may represent grass or reeds.\n\nAs most of the pots had holes in their bottoms, I was led to believe tnat they had\nfallen down from some higher position, probably from wooden boards (as are said to\nexist in the rGya graves). When the irrigation water entered, the boards decayed and\ngave way. As I had previously observed, when examining the graves with Dr. Shawe,\nmost of the pots were filled with human bones. This circumstance seems to indicate that\nthe ancient inhabitants of the Leh valley indulged in the gruesome j)ractico of cutting\nthe corpses to pieces and filling clay pots with the fragments. This custom, which is\nalso found in other parts of the globe, is asserted by the Chinese to have been in vogue\nin the “Empire of the Eastern Women.” Some of the pots had old cracks aird carefully bored holes on both sides of them. Thus the art of mending broken pottery with\nstrings must have been known to the race which built these graves.\n\nThere were, it appears, between fifteen and twenty skulls in one single grave (Plate\nXXVIII, b). How many, exactly, it is difidcult to state now, as w'e were not the first to\nexamine the grave. When we opened a grave in 1903, Dr. Shawe carried homo three\nof the skulls. He took measurements of them and writes with regard to them in his\nletter of the 14tb November 1905, as follows : “ All the skulls I got are very decidedly\negg-shaped. The measurements taken with an ordinary pair of compasses (we have no\nproper ' callipers ’ here) along the antero-posterior and longest transverse diameter of\nthe roof of the skull are (approximately) 6fx5 inches, 6fx5|- inches, and 6fx Scinches, Against these, the similar measmrements of a skull which I got in Baltistan\nfrom a Musulman grave, presumably that of a Balti, are 6|x 6g inches.” If wo convert\nthese measurements into the ordinary centigrade formulas of cephalic indexes, w^e obtain\nthe following numbers ; three skulls from the Leh grave : 74,70 ; 77,77 ; and 77,77.\nBalti skull 82,82. Unfortunately, on our visit to Leh last year, even a pair of compasses could not be obtained, and I therefore cannot give any numbers. But as I\nhave acquired an experienced eye for forms of skulls, I venture to state that all the\nskulls we found in the grave last year, were most distinctly dolichocephalic, and the\nformulas 74 to 77 would probably suit them all. We had also an opportunity to compare them with two skulls taken by Mr. Schmitt from the graves below Leh which date\n\n* This photograph was reproduced in Miss Duncan’s \"A Shimmer Side throv-gTi Western TihetP p, 148, where the painW ornament appears quite distinctly.\n\n» Ind. Ant, Vol. XXXIV, pp. 208 ff.\n\nPlate XXIX.\n\nb. Implements used in devil dances, Leh,\n\nfrom tlie last epidemic of small-pox in Leh, about a hundred years ago. These skulls\nfrom the small-pox graves appeared to be decidedly brachyeephalic, irhen compared with\nthose from the ancient grave. As dolichocephalic heads are a characteristic mark of the\nDards of Hanu, Da, and other Dard places of Ladakh, we are led to believe that the\npeople who built the ancient graves were probably of Dard stock ; at any rate they were\nnot of Tibetan, but of North Indian origin.\n\nBesides human skulls, a head of a sheep, and a horn of an ox were also found in the\ngrave. These are apparently remains of a sacrifice, or gifts to the dead.\n\nThe grave contained also a number of bronze implements, some in fairly good preservation (Plate XXIX, a). Most of them were, however, much corroded, and covered\nwith a thick layer of verdigris. Phst of aU, I may mention small square leaflets of\nthin bronze furnished with an embossed ring, of which we found hundreds. Whether\nthey were used for ornamental purposes, or as coins, I find it impossible to decide. Then\nthere were numerous bronze beads, of round as well as of oblong shape, small and large,\nthe largest thicker than a finger. Later on we discovered little pendants of bronze, of\nbell-like form, with triangular holes and a ring at the top. They were probably inserted\nbetween the bronze beads of the necklace. When we took photos of the bronze implements and other articles, we found a glass bead among the bronze beads. It was of\nmother- o-pearl colour, and looked like Roman or Greek glass. Dr. Marshall informs me,\nhowever, that this kind of glass is found all over Asia.\n\nOnce, when I Had made arrangements to go to the grave and continue my exploration,\nI was prevented from doing so by an attack of malarial fever. Then Mr. and Mrs. Reichel\nof the Moravian Mission .offered to go in my place, and they brought home several more\nvery interesting finds. In particular, there were a number of bronze buttons of various\nsizes with a loop on the reverse. Some of them were of ordinary size, about half an\ninch in diameter, but others were much larger, nearlytwo inches in diameter. The largest\nhad a scalloped edge, like an Indian one-anna piece. None of them contained an inscription. The smallest were quite plain, the largest had an elaborate spiral ornament, and\nthose of medium size, a star ornament. I suppose that these buttons were worn by\nancient officials as a distinguishing mark of rank, just as is the case in China nowadays."

  "passage_text": "Some other round pieces of bronze may have served as mirrors, such as are stBl
found in Ladakh. Some fragments were probably the remains of bronze pots.

On the 28th August, three of our Christians went again to the graves of their own
accord. They found many more bronze implements, several of them in fairly good
preservation ; for instance, a can with a spout of excellent workmanship, though quite
plain and without any ornament ; a seal with a cross-pattern engraved on it; an entire

bracelet with a pattern of little circles. Although we could trace decorative designs on
several fragments, there was no vestige of any script.

In addition let me say that fragments of iron implements came to light also, and
that Mr. and Mrs. Eeichel discovered the only gold article that was in the grave. It is
of a shape similar to the mouthpiece of a trumpet, but its purpose is not known. Its
ornamentation is a curved form of the Greek key.

L

u

After this description of the gra,ve and our finds in it, let me enter into the question
of its date and the nationality of the people who built it. As I have pointed out already,
in connection with the rGya graves, the condition of these graves calls to mind at once
the description of the form of burial practised in the “ Empire of the Eastern Women,”
of the Chinese historians. There we read : “ When a person of rank dies, they strip

off the skin, and put the flesh and bones mixed with gold powder into a vase, and then
bury it At the burial of the sovereign, several tens of the great ministers and rela-

tives are buried at the same time ! ” The latter statement about this gruesome custom
may account for the great number of skulls, sometimes as many as twenty, which are
found in a single grave. As the grave contained large bronze buttons, obviously a mark
of high rank, it is very probable that the Leh grave actually contained the remains of
several “ great ministers.” This “ Empire of the Eastern Women ” has been described
in the Sui sliu, a book which was compiled in c. 586 A.D. Here it is called Nii-Kuo.
Hiuen Tsiang also heard of this empire, and a little after his time, we read that the last
queen died and was replaced by a king. The frontiers of this curious empire are given
by the Sui shu as well as by Hiuen Tsiang. They are : Khotan, Sampaha (Ladakh),
Brahmapura (Chamba State), and Tibet. Erom these definitions we may conclude that
the empire comprised the Tibetan provinces of Guge and Ruthog, and possibly Eastern
Ladakh. The empire was a Tibetan one, according to our Chinese authorities, and it
therefore appears strange that the skulls of the Leh grave are not those of Tibetans, but of
Aryans. My explanation would be that it is very probable that portions of Ladakh were
for a time at least included in this empire. The value of our grave finds lies in this that
they afford us a glimpse of the general state of civilisation which prevailed in this empire. As regards its date, the presence of iron besides bronze precludes the fixing of any
very early date, say before the Christian era. The absence of any form of writing in the
grave would perhaps point to a time earlier than 586 A.D., at which time, according
to the Chinese, the Indian characters were used in the empire. In my opinion the grave
dates from between 1 and 500 A.D.

Eortunately for me, I had finished my investigations, when Mr. Chatterji, Director
of Archseology in the Kashmir State, arrived in Leh with the message that it was the
wish of the Maharaja that no further excavations of any kind should be undertaken in
Kashmir State territory.

The village of Skara {aQa-ra in native documents) is situated south of Leh and forms
a kind of suburb of that- town. On the 3rd September, I visited the ruins of the
sGar-rtse Monastery at Skara. According to K. Marx this is the monastery " for four
lamas only,” founded by King ’aBum-lde, about 500 years ago. It was built on
a crag resembling an elephant. This little monastery was destroyed by the Dogras, at
least so I was told. There was also another small temple erected below the ruin
occupied by one lama who belongs to -the ’aBrug-pa order. Ho tradition regarding
King " aBum-lde has been preserved in the locality.

The village of Skara was formerly situated on a rocky spur to the right of the
Leh valley, where there are still many ruined houses. The chief reason for evacuating

the former site was said to be an epidemic. There are still many grayes in a side-valley
near it.

Probably the most ancient monastery at Skara is the one which is situated in a little
ravine, between the rGar-rtse iMonastery and the ruined village. Pour walls are still
standing, and there are traces of red colour (frescoes) on the walls. Close by is an
underground room, in which we found a human skeleton of recent date.

Below this ruined monastery, there is a mchod-rten shaped like a “ Mon mchod-rten.^'
It consists of a lower square room, on the top of which is placed a round pyramid.
Locally this mchod-rten is known as the grave of a king. It actually contained human
bones, notably fragments of a skull.

Not far from it, on the plain, there is a group of three ancient-looking mchod-rten
of the usual shape. A man from Skara had extracted from them several ancient household utensils filled with grain. Out of these, he sold me a sieve cup made of very thin
copper leaf.

At Skara my attention was drawn to a rather modern-looking round mchod-rten
which was hollow and furnished with a door. Inside of it w’^e found several cremation
tablets of ancient style, some with Indian inscriptions. I was told that a few years ago
an ancient mchod-rten was deslroyed by a Muhammadan who built a house for himself
at Skara. He carried all the tablets found in the old mchod-oden to the new one and
hid them there. In the desert below Skara, there are the low mounds of several ancient
mchod-rten. We found in them cremation tablets with Indian legends, very much like
those at rGya."
}

I was told that in the days of the Ladakhi kings (no\npersona] name could be remembered) two men were ordered to erect this temple as a\npunishment for some crime. No woodwork remains, and there are no traces of images\nor frescoes on the site.\n\nIn the desert east of Leh, there is a large mchod-rten of yellow colour, which is\ncalled Ma-^i-gser-mo. Popular tradition asserts that it is one of the most ancient here.\nOn the western side of the dome there is a niche with a complete figure of a seated\nBuddha. It must formerly have had such niches on all four sides. Attached to it are\ntwo or three mchod-rten of more recent date. One of them was open, and contained\nall sorts of old rubbish, viz., fragments of idols, pages of books, charms, and cremation\ntablets. We took away some of the better preserved tablets. In 1906 we obtained from\nthe same mchod-rten a few sheets of manuscript in a modern Indian dialect which were\nsent to Dr. Vogel, for examination. As King Seng-ge-rnam-rgyal (c. 1600 A.D.) exhibited\nstrong sympathies with the religions of India, the manuscripts may date from his time.\nOf more recent date are the pages of a Sanskrit book in D§vanagari character. One forenoon was\naccordingly set apart for a trip to the top of rNam-rgyal-rts6-mo, Hr. Eeichcl of the\nMoravian Mission accompanying us. He, therefore, concluded a treaty with them, and apparently took their side. He then very cleverly enlisted\nthe energy of the Turkomans on his side, for co-ercing his disobedient vassal\nprinces and unpleasant neighbours. As the\nLadakhi chronicles teU us, the corpses of the slain Turks were placed before the idols\nof the temple of the four Lords {mOon-hhang), This is the reason why the male\nmembers of the royal family of Ladakh are shown wearing the Turkestan dress in the\nfrescoes, whilst the female members are dressed in trae Ladakhi fashion, wearing on\ntheir heads the herag, a leather strap covered with turquoises.\n\nAbove the temple of the four Lords {mGon-hhang) are the ruins of bKra-shis-rnamrgyaTs palace. This book may be identical with\nthe old ‘ palm leaf ’ shown to the Bev. Mr. Bateson on the occasion of his iourney\nthrough Zahgskar in 1908."

to Mon or Lard times (c. 700 — 900 A.L.). The best of them shows a standing Buddha
with Bodhisattvas on Ms right and left (Plate XXXII, a). The one on his right who
carries a vase is Maitreya. The one on his left, and higher up, with a flower in his hand,
is Avalokite^varah Above Mm, in the air, we see two flying figures (Gandharvas ?)
On the reverse of the same stone is a four- armed figure, perhaps a Maitreya, and a
mchod-rten is carved on one of the narrow sides (Plate XXXII, b). I will not now
describe ail the stone sculptures of Leh and surroundings, because it would take too long,
for there are many of them. A number have been mentioned or described in my article,
“ Archaeology in West Tibet.”^ But I will mention another sculpture at Changspa
near a group of houses, lower down, not far from the brook. It is enclosed by a masonry
wall. This figure is furnished with an unusual headdress and seems to represent a
Buddhist priest of the Mon or Lard times.

On a rocky hill to the west of Changspa, there are several crematories and some
ancient mchod-rten. Higher up, on the same hill, are the ruins of the Eibug (Ri-phug)
monastery. As the monastery was reported to be of ancient date, I visited it but could
not, however, discover any inscriptions or documents referring to it. One of the
mchod-rten close by is of an ancient type, but the cremation tablets contained in it
are unfortunately without inscriptions. The temple hall being roofless, nothing remainsof former frescoes except a few traces of colour on the plaster-

The ruined mchod-rten called Teu-bkra-shis-’od-mtho is the laigest in Ladakh. It issituated about 1^- mile from the Commissioner’s compound, a little higher up in the Leh
valley. We measured the circumference of its base at about 10 feet above the ground,
a height at which the masonry rose clear above the surrounding rubbish, and found it to
be 550 feet. It was erected by king ’aBum-lde, in order to cover up a crag which was
believed to be harmful to the country, and is now in a very dilapidated condition.

^ The kneeling figure on the proper left looks more like a human devotee. [ Ed. ]

= Ind. Ant., Vol. XXXY, p 237, and XXXVJ, pp. 85 and 148 ff.

Plate XXXI

-sgo-mang, ancient mchod-rten at Changspa, Leh.

Plate XXXII

On the 9tli September, I went to the Teu-gser-po or Tiserru (as ordinary people call
this ruined mchod-rten), accompanied by Mr. Schmitt of the Moravian Mission, Lobzang,
a Christian and Meteorological Observer at Leh, Pindi Lai, and the Khalasi. Our object
was to study the inside of the structure. When we had climbed up to half its height, we
found a hole in tiie surface, the opening of a narrow shaft. Lobzang went down first o f
all. He came to a narrow room of triangular shape, which was perfectly empty. W e
then tried to dig a new hole in a different place, when suddenly a number of men. who
had been working in the fields, rushed towards us terrified. They implored us not to
open the Tiserru, as such a procedure would bring incalculable misfortune to the
country. From their remonstrances we learned something about the history of the
old monument. The story reminds us of European fairy tales, such as that of the
devil being caught in a bottle. In King ’aBum-lde’s times, there used to live a demon
in a cavity of the rock Teu-gser-po. This devil, who had fire proceeding from his
mouth, roamed about the country and destroyed the king’s palace and portions of the
town of Leh. To exorcise him, the huge stupa was built above his abode. If we opened
the stupa, the people feared that the evil spirit which had been kept under custody for
500 years, might once more attain liberty. We pointed to the old holes in the building,
and observed that he might have escaped long ago. But that was of no avail. At the
same time, we were told that the old stupa was not only a repository for devils, but for
heavy gales also. When in the days of King ’aBum-lde, the country suffered severely
from storms, several largo clay pots were held against the wind with their mouths
open. As soon as the wind subsided, their mouths were closed, and they were stored
up in the stupa with the storms contained in them. People were afraid we might find
and open this ancient pottery, and that the country would be plagued with heavy gales
again.

From the opposition which we met in this case from the peasants of Leh, it was
plain to me that it is difficult to do archaeological work in an inhabited country. The
chronicles of Ladakh have only a very short note on this mohod-rten. They simply
state that it was built, because “ some fatality ” had occurred at Leh. I am still of
opinion that the idea of a devil living in this place has something to do with the ancient
graves described above. These graves are situated in proximity to, and some of them
possibly below the mohod-rten.

On the same day, I went higher up the Leh valley, following the desert road
to the w'^est of the cultivated area, accompanied by Pindi Lai and the Khalasi. Close to
the village of dG-onpa, we passed by the ruined site of an old town with mchod-rten of
ancient type near it. There we found also a stone sculpture of some Bodhisattva, enin a masonry wall, with a IhatJio (altar of the pre-Buddhist religion), in front of
it (Plate XXXIV, a). As usual, the altar was furnished with many ibex horns. This
ruined town may be the original site of the present village of dGonpa.

Marching upwards in the side-valley to the left of the village of dGonpa, we
came to the ruins of an ancient temple, which is generally known by the name of
Gya-mthsa. I had visited it occasionally, ten or twelve years ago, when I was stationed"

Five miles below Leh, at Spithug (dPe-thub ; map Pittuk), the road\npasses by the rook, on which King ’aBum-lde built his famous monastery 500 years ago.\nThis monastery can be entered only with special permission of the aKu-shog'^ and\nas such a sKu-shog was not present at Leh, we had to give up the idea of visiting it. On\nthe top of the same rock can be seen also the ruins of some older building, i)robably a\ncastle. On the plain below, we found a ruined mchod-rten of ancient typo, which\ncontained cremation tablets of the shape of miniature stupas. These tablets had an\ninscription in Indian characters impressed on them. Pandit Mukund Bam of Kashmir,\nto whom we showed such a tablet, was fortunately able to read the inscription. It\nagain contains the Ye dharma formula, which in this case is written in an early type\nof Devanagari characters, say, of the 11th or 12th century A.H. On the western\nprominence of the rock we noticed several very flat relievos, representing bTsong-kha-pa\nand his disciples. It will be remembered that the Spithug monastery was erected in\nhonour of that reformer. This type of relievo which probably dates from the 15th or\n16th century, is very different from the old type as it is represented at Leh and\nChangspa. The new type reminds us of the flat, carved figures often found on slabs\nplaced on walls.\n\nThe trade road passes through the lowest extremity of the village of Phyang. This\nis a pity, for the village is well worth a visit. I should have visited it, in spite of everything, if at the time of our expedition, the thought had dawned upon me, that Phyang\n\n^ sKu-shog, tlie incarnation of its first abbot.\n\n(spelt Phyi-dhang ; map Pliayang) is probably tbe most ancient town of Western\nTibet. It was\nerected by King bKra.shis-rnam-rgyal (c. 1500—1532 A.D.) and belongs to the ’aBrikhung-pa sect of lamas. This monastery comes into view when the plain on the right\nbank of the Phyang brook is reached. At this place King bKra-shis-rnam-rgyal raised\na long flagstaff on an elaborate pedestal. As we know from the chronicles, this flagstaff\nwas intended to serve as a place of refuge for aU those who were guilty of a orimen Icbscb\nmajestatis. Had he not plucked out his elder brother’s eyes\nand deprived him of his royal power? No doubt, bKra-sMs himself had good reason to\nembrace the flagstaff most cordially. mohocl-rten and mcliod-rten gates with four doors. Several of them contain pictures similar to those noticed at Basgo and Ubshi, i.e., Buddha-like figures of blue complexion.
They probably represent Nagas, and these gates and mchod-rten may be of Bonpo
origin. But there were so many that it was found impossible to register them all.

Let me add a few words with regard to Tibetan palaeography, based on a comparison of the Alchi and Tabo inscriptions of the 11th century. Besides the Alchi and Tabo
mscriptions of the 11th century, the following datable inscriptions of ancient Tibet are
known : (1) The Endere manuscripts, excavated by Sir M. A. Stein in Turkestan.

The latest date which can be attributed to them is the year 788 A.D., but several appear
to be earlier. (2) The inscription of Khri-srong-lde-btsan in Lhasa of c. 780 A.D.
discovered and edited by Dr. Waddell.^ (3) The inscription of king Eal-pa-can in Lhasa,
of c. 810-820 A.D."

The most archaic of the Endere relics have the following peculiarities : —

(1) The i vowel sign is often inverted.

(2) In several cases, the final consonant of a syllable is written below the first.

(3) The article is in many cases pha and pho, instead of the ordinary pa
and po.

(4) Ordinary c and ts are in many oases replaced by oh and ths ; and ch and ths
both have y, 6, and d prefixes attached to them.

(5) When m precedes iov e, y intervenes.

(6) Words ending in r, I, or n, are furnished with a d suf&x, called drag.

If we examine the Tabo, Poo and Alchi inscriptions of the 11th century, with regard to the peculiarities of the Endere manuscripts enumerated above, we find that they
exhibit only the two last mentioned peculiarities, viz., y intervenes between m and ior m
and e ; and r, I, and n are often furnished with a d suffix. Thus we see that during the
period from the 8th to the llth century, the Tibetan orthography has come much nearer
to its present state. The i vowel sign, for instance, is no more found inverted, but always
in its present position. At Alchi we found the i vowel sign only once inverted and that
was probably due to want of space. From this observation we may conclude that all
those inscriptions which contain inverted i vowel signs, may be older than the llth
century. As regards the position of the[e and o vowel signs on the right or left upper
end, or above the consonant base, it varies with the age of inscriptions. I am of opinion
that the compilation of the hKa-’agywr and hStan- agyw)', in c. 1300 A.D., marks an
epoch in Tibetan palaeography. It probably put an end to the intervening y between
m and i or e, and to the suffixed d. From the year 1300 A.D. onwards Tibetan orthography presumably remained stationary, and the age of an inscription after 1300 A.D.
<®n be estimated only by the form of its compound letters, and the position of vowel
signs on or above their consonant bases.

On our way back, from Alcbi to Saspola, I visiteci tlie site of a ruined castle called
AlcM-inkhar-gog, which once guarded the Alchi bridge. I found a number of sherds of
pottery with dark red designs. The pottery was not wheel-made, but rudely shaped with
the hand. As will be remembered, entire specimens of pottery with dark red designs
were found in the ancient graves at Leh. On the boulders round about the ruined castle
are found many inscriptions of officers who once resided here. As I have shown in my
article “ Archseology in Western Tibet, ” most of these epigraphs may be attributed to
the times of King Nyi-ma-mgon, in the 10th century, and his immediate successors. We
took a photo of one of them.

On the 24th September, the principal caravan under Pincli Lai, marched to sNyurla,
by the ordinary road. I myself went to sGyera on the left bank of the Indus, accompanied by Puntsog, my assistant, and Labpa, the Khansaman. Prom s Gy era, I went up
■the valley, to visit the famous monastery of Mang-rgyu. Just below it, we passed a very
rudely-executed rock sculpture which represents Mahju^ri. The inscription below it
mentions King Phun-thsogs-rnam-rgyal of the 18th century. It is the latest rock
sculpture in West Tibet which I have seen.

The Mang-rgyu monastery consists of four temples standing in a row, with their
doors towards the East like so many others of the same period.

(1) Byams-chen (or Loke^vara). — This temple contains a huge stucco image ; but
the present lamas are uncertain whether it represents Maitreya or Avalokite^vara. I
should think that it represents the former. The door is furnished with ancient wood
narvings of Indian type.

(2) ’aDu-khang (or Thugs-rje-chen-po). — The door of this temple is ornamented with
ancient wood carvings of artistic workmanship, which represent the five Dhyani-buddhas
with Vairochana (rNam-par-snang-mdzad) in the centre. We found an ancient and
much effaced inscription in this hall near the door. I ordered it to be copied. Neither
a personal nor a local name has been preserved in it, and it contains hardly a
single coherent sentence. But the preserved fragments afford several instances of
intervening y between m and i, and for this reason I feel inclined to attribute it to the
11th or 12th century. Local tradition connects the Mang-rgyu monastery with Lama
Ein-chen-bzang-po. In another part of the same hall, we found a short fragmentary
inscription giving the name of a forgotten prince, possibly a younger son of one of the
kings of the first dynasty of Ladakh. It reads Jo-no-ohmg-Khri-stod-’adi, the younger prince Khri-stod.”"
